lines.text: 3.8 Millets: The Grains That Came Back
Jowar, bajra, ragi, sanwa, kodo, kutki — these are
millets, and they are among the oldest cultivated
grains in India. For centuries they were ordinary
food across large parts of the country. Then, within
a few decades, they largely disappeared from
urban plates, pushed aside by polished rice and
refined wheat.
They are coming back, and the reason is nutrition.
Millets are small-grained cereals, so they supply
carbohydrate like any cereal. What sets them apart
is what comes with the carbohydrate: substantially
more dietary fibre than polished rice, along with
iron, calcium and B vitamins. Because of this they
are often called nutri-cereals — cereals that carry
protective nutrients alongside energy.
Millets are also easier on the land. They grow in
poor soil, tolerate Iow and unreliable rainfall, and
need far less water than rice. In a country where
groundwater is falling in many districts, a grain
that produces food on a fraction of the water is
not a minor advantage.
So a millet does three useful things at once: it
feeds a person better than polished rice, it grows
where rice will not, and it uses less water doing it.

Would millets alone be enough?
No — and the reason is worth understanding. Millets are strong on carbohydrate,
fibre and several minerals, but weak on some nutrients the body needs, and no
cereal supplies everything.
Eaten with dal, vegetables, milk or curd, millets make an excellent meal. Eaten
alone, they leave gaps.
This is true of every single food, however good: the balance is in the plate,
never in the item.
